title: The Five-Minute Strike
passages:
Senn checked the chronometer. Four minutes and eleven seconds until the chime, which meant four minutes to look busy before Voss relieved them at the console. They tapped the board, bringing up the thermal envelope for Relay Bay Seven. Nothing to report, same as the last shift, same as the shift before that, according to the log they weren’t allowed to read yet. Past logs only. The station’s rules, not theirs.

"Still staring at the same ghost heat signature?" Voss asked, drifting through the hatch with a coffee bulb clamped between her teeth. She pulled it free with a pop. "Bay Seven’s been cold since commissioning. The ghosts are just condensation."

"It’s a pattern," Senn said. "Every five minutes, on the chime, there’s a spike. Minimal, but regular. Someone’s cycling something in there, and they’re not logging it."

Voss handed over the slate. Senn scrolled past filter scrubs and a complaint about lukewarm nutrient paste and stopped at the last page. Handwriting they didn’t recognize, in ink, which no one used anymore: *Don’t trust the chime. It doesn’t just mark shifts. It resets us.*

"What is that?" Senn asked.

"Your note," Voss said. "You leave it for yourself every shift. Then you wipe and forget. I find it touching. Like a terrible relationship with yourself."

The clock struck.

Senn felt the tug behind the eyes, the soft erasure of the last five minutes. They blinked. Voss was holding the slate out, expectant. "Your shift. Initial the handoff."

Senn looked at the chronometer. Four minutes and eleven seconds until the chime. They tapped the board. Relay Bay Seven showed nothing unusual.

"Cold since commissioning," Senn said.

"Exactly," Voss said, and took the slate back.

Voss flipped the slate over, her thumb brushing the fresh ink that hadn’t been there a moment before. *The chime isn’t a reset; it’s a record. Someone died in Bay Seven, and the wipe erases the evidence.* She stared, eyes narrowing, then tucked the slate into her belt as the low hum of the station grew louder. Four minutes and eleven seconds ticked down, and the chime’s metallic ring vibrated through the metal floor. Senn’s vision blurred at the edges, the familiar tug behind the eyes pulling the last five minutes into oblivion. In that split second, a flash of movement caught their eye—a dark shape slipping past the coolant pipes of Bay Seven, its suit reflecting the dim red warning lights before vanishing as the memory dissolved. The chime struck, and the station exhaled. When Senn’s eyes cleared, Voss was already at the console, slate in hand, tapping the handoff. ‘Your shift. Initial the handoff,’ she said, voice flat. Senn reached for the stylus, hesitated, then wrote their initials, the ink already fading from the page they could not remember having written.
